explanation.surface: Cats were first kept as pets in a remote Russian town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kept in' looks like a container signal, but 'in' is only a link and 'kept' supplies its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tomsk is an old university city in western Siberia, on the Tom river in Russia.

clue.text: Weapon European leader kept in box

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter of the word is taken
what is kept in something is held within it, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: to spar is to box
first letter of European

explanation.surface: A European head of state keeps a weapon locked in a case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' looks like a container, but it is the verb, boxing in training.
explanation.definitionFit: A spear is a long pole with a pointed tip used for thrusting or throwing, one of the oldest arms.

clue.text: Panel team designed, giving identification on door?

indicators.note: something designed has been planned and put together, so the letters are arranged afresh

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A design team produces a sign for an office door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Panel' looks like part of the door, but it is merely letters for rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: A nameplate is a small plaque bearing a person's name, typically fixed to an office door; the question mark flags an example.

clue.text: Russian girl, one at home in Burlington House

indicators.note: being in something means being inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
Burlington House in Piccadilly is the home of the RA, the Royal Academy of Arts
at home means in

explanation.surface: A Russian woman feels at ease in a grand London mansion.
explanation.walkthrough: Burlington House is the London building that houses the Royal Academy of Arts, so it stands for RA.
explanation.definitionFit: Irina is a common Russian female first name, so it answers the general description.

clue.text: Gap left by cutter observed at entrance

blocks.note: saw is the past tense of see, to observe
a gate is an entrance

explanation.surface: A hole left by a burglar's tool was spotted at the gate.
explanation.walkthrough: The observing verb in the wordplay is spelt the same as the cutting tool in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw gate, or kerf, is the slit made by a blade as it cuts through timber.

clue.text: Part of Canada our country invested in over there

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: for a British setter, our country is the UK
yon is an old word for that one over there

explanation.surface: British money has been put into a region across the Atlantic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our country' is from the point of view of The Times, a British paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Yukon is a territory in north-west Canada bordering Alaska, one of the country's three territories.

clue.text: It’s fine for example to go outside and meet

indicators.note: going outside something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: say is used to introduce an example
'tis is an old contraction of it is
F is the pencil abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: Someone decides that going outside to meet up is fine.
explanation.walkthrough: The inner pieces come first in the clue but go inside the outer one; F for fine is from pencil grading.
explanation.definitionFit: To meet a requirement is to fulfil it, which is also what the verb satisfy means with a demand or need.

clue.text: One dispatches ungulates crossing east part of this ancient city

indicators.note: in an across entry east is the right-hand side, so only the word's final letter is taken
to cross something is to span it, so one piece stretches round the others

blocks.note: deer are hoofed mammals, or ungulates
last letter of this
Troy is the ancient city of Homer's Iliad

explanation.surface: A hunter dispatches deer crossing the eastern part of an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East' looks like the usual E, but here it picks the right-hand end of the next word. 'One dispatches' is a noun phrase: someone who kills.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispatch is to kill, so a destroyer is one who dispatches or wipes things out.
